purpose: Verbatim assignment metadata from current later-course pages; source-baseline allocations, not released lesson packets or verified reading assets

records.title: Basic logical notions
records.source_text: Part I, chapters 1–3. Explain validity, soundness, consistency, and equivalence using original examples. For each chapter, complete four varied exercises, check after attempting them, and record conceptual errors.

records.title: Truth-functional syntax and symbolization
records.source_text: Part II, chapters 4–8. Practise main connectives, brackets, inclusive disjunction, material conditional, and ambiguity. Complete at least twenty-four short symbolizations, including translation back into English. Compare two plausible formalizations of an ambiguous sentence.

records.title: Truth-functional semantics
records.source_text: Part III, chapters 9–15. Construct complete and abbreviated truth tables, classify sentences and arguments, and provide countervaluations. Complete at least sixteen problems spanning validity, equivalence, and consistency. Explain one countervaluation in prose.

records.title: Natural deduction for truth-functional logic
records.source_text: Part IV, chapters 16–22. Work through one example per new rule, then a partially completed proof, then independent mixed practice. Complete at least twenty proofs including conditional proof, indirect proof, and nested assumptions. For five proofs, write a strategy paragraph before using a checker.

records.title: First-order language
records.source_text: Part V, chapters 23–29. Domains, predicates, quantifiers, scope, identity, and multiple quantification. Complete twenty-four symbolizations with domain declarations. Explain the difference between “everyone admires someone” and “someone is admired by everyone” using a small diagram.

records.title: Interpretations and countermodels
records.source_text: Part VI, chapters 30–35. Build finite interpretations, assess quantified sentences, and distinguish inability to find a countermodel from proof of validity. Complete twelve interpretation/countermodel tasks and explain two in ordinary prose.

records.title: First-order natural deduction
records.source_text: Part VII, chapters 36–41. Complete sixteen mixed proofs covering quantifier rules, identity, and rule restrictions. Make an error card for each recurring misuse of a name, variable, or undischarged assumption. Use Carnap only in the same supported calculus; a plain written solution with the book’s rules is sufficient.

records.title: Transfer and independent assessment
records.source_text: Formalize one short philosophical argument and write 800–1,000 words about interpretive choices and limitations. Complete an unaided mixed assessment with translations, semantic tests, truth-functional proofs, quantified proofs, and a countermodel. Explain two proof strategies orally or in text, then complete a smaller fresh set after a delay. Assessment and delayed work are included in the sixteen hours.

records.title: Historical orientation and method
records.source_text: Revisit Apology 20c–23c and Meno 80d–86c. Consult OpenStax 4.2 “Classical Philosophy” for Greek context ([<u>https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/4-2-classical-philosophy</u>](https://openstax.org/books/introduction-philosophy/pages/4-2-classical-philosophy)). Create a one-page chronology separating approximate author dates, dramatic settings, and composition where the sources actually establish them; mark unsupported dates uncertain. Use OpenStax for broad orientation, and verify exact quotations in a primary text. Its incidental description of the opening sentence of Aristotle’s Metaphysics is inaccurate; the primary opening is I.1, 980a21 ([<u>https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.1.i.html</u>](https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.1.i.html)). This quotation check is only needed if you use that remark, not an extra assigned book. Write 400 words on why a dialogue character’s assertion is not automatically Plato’s doctrine.

records.title: The challenge of justice
records.source_text: Republic I and II through 367e. Map Thrasymachus’ and Glaucon’s challenges separately. Output: a 600-word reconstruction of the strongest challenge and a written explanation of what a successful answer would need to show.

records.title: Plato’s answer and its limits
records.source_text: Republic IV 427d–445e and IX 577c–580c. Reconstruct the city–soul comparison and the relation between psychic order and justice. PC activity: identify every premise needed to move from an account of justice to the claim that being just benefits its possessor. This supplies the answer omitted from the old reading list.

records.title: Knowledge and the soul
records.source_text: Republic VI 509d–511e, VII 514a–521b; Phaedo 64a–69e, 72e–84b. Distinguish images from arguments. Write 700 words evaluating either recollection or affinity, including what the selected argument is intended to establish.

records.title: Aristotle on explanation
records.source_text: Categories 1–5 and Physics II.1–3, II.8. Classify the explanatory questions asked about one natural object and one artifact. Write a 500-word comparison of substance and attribute, then assess one argument about teleology without importing modern biological assumptions silently.

records.title: Aristotle and Hellenistic alternatives
records.source_text: De Anima II.1–3; Epicurus 122–135; Sextus I.1–30. Explain why “soul” need not mean an immaterial ghost. Compare Epicurus on death with Socrates’ argument in Apology, and identify what suspension of judgment is meant to do. These are bounded encounters, not complete courses in Hellenistic philosophy.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,500–1,800 words on one question: “Does Republic IV answer Glaucon’s challenge?”; “Does the affinity argument support immortality?”; or “Does Aristotle’s soul account avoid the problems of the model it opposes?” Include outline, draft, feedback, revision, and memo.

records.title: Independent assessment and later recall
records.source_text: Interpret an unseen short passage from the assigned corpus with the source visible; explain one comparison without notes; answer a new objection to the essay; complete a delayed reconstruction in the next course. Ready means accurate textual work and relevant reasoning on new material, not memorizing every author’s dates.

records.title: Context and transmission
records.source_text: Read the anthology’s general introduction and source introductions. Map the languages, institutions, translation movements, and intellectual settings actually supported by these introductions. Label the scope as the Arabic/Islamic context supplied by this source; mark missing Latin/Jewish contextual details as questions rather than filling them from an AI’s recollection. Output: a sourced 500-word explanation of why a simple “faith versus reason” storyline is inadequate.

records.title: Time and experience
records.source_text: Augustine XI.14–31. Reconstruct the puzzle of past, present, and future. PC activity: distinguish a claim about temporal reality from a claim about measuring time. Write a 400-word objection and possible response.

records.title: Anselm and Gaunilo
records.source_text: Assigned Proslogion and replies. Produce parallel reconstructions, separating the original argument, parody, and response. Explain whether the parody targets the strongest reading. Do not simply label an argument “ontological” and assume that settles its validity.

records.title: Avicenna on self and soul
records.source_text: Assigned On the Soul excerpt. Describe the thought experiment’s assumptions, conclusion, and limits; compare Aristotle and Descartes cautiously. Write a 600-word interpretive exercise grounded in the actual translation.

records.title: Al-Ghazali and philosophical inquiry
records.source_text: Assigned anthology excerpt of Rescuer. Identify distinctions among mathematical, logical, physical, metaphysical, political, and ethical investigations where the text makes them. Write a 500-word analysis of an argument against philosophers, distinguishing autobiography, classification, and demonstration.

records.title: Maimonides and Aquinas
records.source_text: Guide I.50–60; Summa I q.1 a.8 and q.2 aa.1–3. Compare negative predication with one of Aquinas’s arguments. Map the objection–response form of a Summa article. Do not assimilate all theological arguments to one generic proof.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,500–1,800 words: “What, exactly, does Avicenna’s thought experiment establish?”; “Does Gaunilo answer Anselm?”; or “Can negative theology make informative claims?” Include one competing interpretation and a justified textual decision.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Analyze a fresh assigned passage, compare two methods of argument, explain an unanticipated objection, and later reconstruct the essay’s key inference. Remediate contextual misattributions by returning to the source introduction and passage before repeating the task.

records.title: Doubt, the thinker, and representation
records.source_text: Reread Meditations I–II and read III. Trace what each stage has established. Output: an annotated argument map and 500-word account of one contested inference.

records.title: God, error, and the world
records.source_text: Meditations IV–VI. Write 700 words explaining the strongest version of the circle objection and a possible response. A tutorial asks what depends on clear and distinct perception and what depends on divine reliability.

records.title: Embodiment and interaction
records.source_text: Read the five dated letters. Create a correspondence map showing objection, reply, reformulation, and unresolved issue. Output: 500 words on whether Descartes answers Elisabeth’s question rather than a different question.

records.title: Substance and explanation
records.source_text: Spinoza’s assigned passages and Leibniz’s Monadology. Reconstruct one argument for a substantive metaphysical claim from each. Compare explanatory aims before evaluating their conclusions.

records.title: Ideas and qualities
records.source_text: Locke and Berkeley. Use an ordinary object to distinguish primary/secondary qualities and ideas/objects. Write 600 words assessing a premise in Berkeley’s argument, with a charitable Locke comparison.

records.title: Hume’s challenge
records.source_text: Enquiry II–VII and XII. Separate the skeptical argument about induction, the “skeptical solution,” the account of necessary connection, and mitigated skepticism. PC activity: map where a proposed defense of induction risks circularity.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,000 words on the Cartesian circle, Elisabeth’s objection, Berkeley’s anti-abstraction argument, or Hume’s account of induction. Use at least two exact passages and one checked scholarly interpretation, selected through the reference protocol below.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Independent passage interpretation plus a comparison not rehearsed in the essay, followed by a brief defense and delayed reconstruction. If comparison becomes a list of slogans, return to a shared question and state each author’s actual premise and conclusion.

records.title: Moral questions and reasoning
records.source_text: Revisit Singer’s argument and read OpenStax 8.1–8.3 for vocabulary. Separate a factual dispute, a normative claim, and a metaethical question. Write a 400-word case analysis with assumptions explicit.

records.title: Character and flourishing
records.source_text: Aristotle I.1–10, II.1–9, VI.1–5. Reconstruct the function argument and explain practical wisdom. Create an example in which applying the mean requires judgment rather than arithmetic.

records.title: Moral cultivation across contexts
records.source_text: Mengzi 2A6 and 6A1–10. Explain the sprouts analogy and one rival interpretation of “human nature.” Write 600 words comparing an aspect of moral development with Aristotle while stating a limit of the comparison.

records.title: Duty and autonomy
records.source_text: Groundwork I–II. Reconstruct a universal-law test and distinguish treating a person as a means from merely as a means. Test the argument on a fresh maxim before reading a commentator’s response.

records.title: Welfare and justification
records.source_text: Mill II and IV. Compare quality and quantity of pleasure, then reconstruct the proof. Output: a 600-word objection and reply on “desired” and “desirable,” with the inferential claim made precise.

records.title: Moral language and applied argument
records.source_text: Hume 3.1.1, Ayer VI, Thomson’s article. Explain the is/ought passage and emotivism without assuming Hume and Ayer have the same project. Analyze one Thomson thought experiment, distinguishing the conclusion it supports from a broader conclusion it does not establish.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,000 words defending a bounded verdict on one core argument or applying two theories to a precisely specified case. Prompts: “Can Kant’s universal-law test identify the relevant wrong?”; “Does Mill’s proof justify utility as the ultimate end?”; “Does Thomson’s argument establish the conclusion commonly attributed to it?”

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Independently distinguish three theory types, interpret a new passage, and assess a changed case. Disagreement with a moral conclusion is not a grading error; unsupported interpretation or inference is. Remedy a theory-confusion by reconstructing its premises before revisiting applications.

records.title: Knowledge and justification
records.source_text: Gettier and Goldman. Create a map distinguishing an analysis of knowledge from an account of justified belief. Write 600 words evaluating one reliability condition using a new case.

records.title: Testimony and trust
records.source_text: Hume X Part I and Reid VI.24. Explain the disagreement over the grounds of trusting others, avoiding the claim that all testimony is about miracles. PC activity: vary source reliability, dependence among witnesses, and background evidence in a case matrix. State what the comparison does not decide.

records.title: Epistemic injustice
records.source_text: Fricker chapter 1. Reconstruct testimonial injustice and compare it with ordinary error or deception. Write a 600-word case analysis with a counterexample to an overbroad definition. Hermeneutical injustice is an optional later topic, not assessed from an unread chapter.

records.title: Persons and continuity
records.source_text: Locke II.xxvii and Parfit’s article. Map body, memory, psychological continuity, and numerical identity. Explain the role of fission without assuming that imaginative possibility alone settles metaphysical possibility.

records.title: A different inquiry into self
records.source_text: SN 22.59 and the four specified IEP “Buddha” sections. Identify the five aggregates, the argument’s structure, and the practical purpose of the discourse. Mark one claim directly supported by Sujato’s SN 22.59 and one stronger interpretive claim made by the IEP guide. The guide is a scholarly interpretation, not a neutral answer key; disagreement with it is not automatically a textual error. Write 700 words comparing a narrowly specified question with Locke while explaining why the projects are not interchangeable. Do not recast “not-self” automatically as a Western bundle theory.

records.title: Freedom and responsibility
records.source_text: Frankfurt and van Inwagen. Reconstruct the principle of alternate possibilities, a Frankfurt case, and the consequence argument. Diagram which assumptions differ, then write 600 words on whether an objection attacks determinism, alternate possibilities, or a transfer principle.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,200 words on testimony, reliabilism, identity, or responsibility. Include one verified secondary interpretation and one serious rival argument. State clearly whether your paper is interpretive, conceptual, or normative.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Interpret a new assigned passage, construct a fresh counterexample, and answer an unscripted objection. If two positions are being conflated, make a question–premise–conclusion comparison before retesting. Retention is checked in science or the selected area course.

records.title: Authority and method
records.source_text: Hobbes 13–15. Separate prudential motivation, moral obligation, and institutional authority. Write 500 words on what the state-of-nature argument assumes.

records.title: Consent and property
records.source_text: Hobbes 17; Locke’s assigned passages. Map the labor/property argument and the consent claim. Compare a specific premise rather than summarizing “Hobbes versus Locke” in general.

records.title: Liberty and expression
records.source_text: Mill I–II. Apply the harm principle to two carefully described cases, then explain the argument for hearing contrary opinions. PC activity: distinguish a claim’s truth, the right to express it, and the justification for a particular restriction.

records.title: Equal standing and education
records.source_text: Wollstonecraft II and Du Bois I. Write 700 words reconstructing one author’s account of a barrier to equal agency or recognition. Discuss interpretive risks in treating autobiographical, literary, and historical forms as mere illustrations.

records.title: Fairness and entitlement
records.source_text: Rawls and Nozick. Reconstruct the original-position argument and the Wilt Chamberlain objection; identify where principles are selected and where institutions are evaluated. Build a small numerical distribution example, explaining why arithmetic alone cannot decide justice.

records.title: Contract and exclusion
records.source_text: Mills introduction and chapter 1. Compare a descriptive claim about actual institutions with a normative claim about legitimate ones. Write 700 words on whether Mills revises, rejects, or repurposes the social-contract framework, with evidence.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,200 words on a bounded issue: a consent argument, the limits of Mill’s speech argument, Rawls versus Nozick on a specified distribution, or Mills’s challenge to ideal theory. Represent the strongest relevant opposing view before defending a conclusion.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Analyze a new political case, identify which factual questions need evidence, and defend one principle under a changed circumstance. Remediate a factual/normative conflation before reassessing. Political agreement with a tutor is never a readiness criterion.

records.title: Kant’s question and vocabulary
records.source_text: Prolegomena §§1–5 and B Preface selection. Build a concept sheet with examples and nonexamples. Explain why “a priori” does not simply mean “innate” or “obvious.”

records.title: Space and experience
records.source_text: Prolegomena §§6–13. Reconstruct one argument concerning intuition; distinguish transcendental conditions from psychological reports. Write 600 words testing a possible objection.

records.title: Objectivity and causation
records.source_text: Prolegomena §§14–30; Second Analogy A189/B232–A211/B256. Distinguish a succession of perceptions from perception of an objective succession. Create a paired-case diagram, then explain which premise establishes a necessary rule. The exact passage supports the course’s answer-to-Hume outcome.

records.title: Limits of metaphysics
records.source_text: Prolegomena §§57–60. Explain the distinction between the legitimate use of concepts and overextension. Write 500 words on what the critical project permits and limits; do not infer that Kant simply rejects all metaphysics.

records.title: Recognition
records.source_text: Hegel §§178–196 and the bounded SEP section 3.1.1 passage specified above. Trace dependence and reversal in lordship and bondage. Write a 700-word interpretation distinguishing the argument’s place in the work from a later political application.

records.title: Alienation and genealogy
records.source_text: Marx’s two texts and Nietzsche First Essay. Write two 500-word reconstructions, then compare what counts as a philosophical explanation. A genealogy is not automatically a refutation merely because it explains a belief’s origin.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,200 words on Kant’s Second Analogy, Hegelian recognition, Marxian alienation, or a specified Nietzschean genealogical claim. Use the exact primary passage and a checked specialist commentary; acknowledge a competing interpretation.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Interpret an unfamiliar short passage from the set and compare two methods of inquiry. If the course becomes terminology recall, return to a single argument and state what would follow if its premise were false.

records.title: Induction and confirmation
records.source_text: Hume IV–V and Hempel chapter 2. Reconstruct the induction problem and a hypothetico-deductive testing scheme. PC activity: distinguish P(evidence given hypothesis) from P(hypothesis given evidence) using a small invented frequency table. A six-hour probability bridge is available if needed and is additional to the course estimate.

records.title: Testing and falsifiability
records.source_text: Popper chapter 1. Explain the role of risky predictions and auxiliary assumptions. Write 600 words on why one apparently contrary observation does not automatically dictate abandonment of a theory.

records.title: Scientific explanation
records.source_text: Hempel chapter 5. Reconstruct an explanation schema and test it with an original case. Identify an explanatory direction or relevance problem, then explain whether it defeats the whole approach or a specific formulation.

records.title: Change in science
records.source_text: Kuhn II, VI, VII, IX. Distinguish normal science, anomaly, crisis, and revolution without turning them into a simple inevitable cycle. Write 700 words on a selected claim about theory change.

records.title: Realism and empirical adequacy
records.source_text: Van Fraassen chapter 2 §§1–3. State what accepting a theory commits one to under each view. Compare an inference to the best explanation with an empiricist reply using a carefully bounded example.

records.title: Objectivity and scientific communities
records.source_text: Longino chapter 4 and the complete bounded case packet. Read the SPM’s footnote 4 before using confidence and likelihood terms. In Gillett’s abstract, identify the stated method and claim, then state what cannot be evaluated without the full paper. Identify evidence, assumptions, value judgments, uncertainty language, and routes for criticism. Do not infer that values make every conclusion arbitrary or that consensus makes criticism unnecessary.

records.title: Case paper and revision
records.source_text: Write 1,800–2,200 words on one philosophical issue in the packet, or on an equivalently documented scientific case chosen from public primary sources. Use at least one course argument and distinguish what the scientific source actually shows from your interpretation. A case packet for an alternative must be bounded and accessible before the paper begins.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Analyze a new claim about testing or uncertainty, reconstruct one argument without notes, and defend the case paper under a changed assumption. If source comprehension is weak, consult a domain introduction rather than invent an answer; the tutor must flag unresolved scientific facts.

records.title: Context and reading practice
records.source_text: Read the two bounded SEP context selections above. Create a provisional Warring States context map and begin a glossary of ren, li, yi, de, dao, and xing. Add a primary passage and alternative rendering as each term is encountered in Modules 2–6; the ten-hour opening module does not require mastering all six in advance. Do not treat a glossary entry as a final definition.

records.title: Analects
records.source_text: Read the specified books. Choose four connected sayings and reconstruct an account of cultivation or governing. Write 700 words explaining how an aphoristic text can support a philosophical interpretation without forcing it into an imaginary continuous treatise.

records.title: Mengzi
records.source_text: Read the assigned passages. Examine the sprouts, human nature, and the extension of concern. Write 700 words on one argument and a textual difficulty. Revisit Aristotle only after representing Mengzi in his own terms.

records.title: Mohist challenge
records.source_text: Read Mozi 16. Reconstruct the argument for impartial care and a likely Confucian objection. PC activity: distinguish impartial concern, identical treatment, and absence of personal relationships. Identify which claim the text actually requires.

records.title: Zhuangzi
records.source_text: Read chapters 1–3 and 6. Trace the role of story, perspective, skill, and transformation. Compare two interpretations of one passage and explain their evidence. Do not assume that a story is either a literal doctrine or philosophically empty literature.

records.title: Xunzi
records.source_text: Read chapters 1 and 23. Reconstruct a disagreement with Mengzi, including the work done by “nature,” deliberate effort, ritual, and learning. Write 800 words that distinguishes disagreement from a translation-generated appearance of disagreement.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words: “Is the Mengzi–Xunzi disagreement primarily about motivation, development, or the meaning of nature?”; “Does Mozi’s argument require abandoning special relationships?”; or “What does a selected Zhuangzi passage justify about knowledge or perspective?” Include one specialist secondary interpretation and a translation note.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Independently interpret a fresh assigned passage, compare two thinkers without using a European thinker as the default measure, and defend a translation-sensitive claim. A subsequent cross-tradition comparison must state both a productive connection and a limit.

records.title: Context and method
records.source_text: Read Wiredu’s essay, Du Bois’s “The Forethought,” and the bounded Fanon context reading named above. Write 600 words on a bad comparison and how to repair it. Identify the language, region, historical setting, and kind of claim relevant to each author.

records.title: Du Bois on self and social life
records.source_text: Souls I and III. Interpret double consciousness and the education/politics dispute. Map the roles of narrative, history, and argument. Output: a 700-word reading with exact textual support.

records.title: Fanon on racialized experience
records.source_text: Read chapter 5 in full, returning to the finite SEP context passage as needed. Distinguish the lived description from the claims about social structures it supports. Compare a narrow point with Du Bois while preserving historical differences.

records.title: Personhood and community
records.source_text: Menkiti and Gyekye in full. Reconstruct their positions and identify where personhood is descriptive, normative, acquired, or presupposed. PC activity: test a single case under each interpretation rather than attach blanket “individualist” and “collectivist” labels.

records.title: Institutions and critique
records.source_text: Mills chapter 2, with Course 8’s chapter 1 available for reference. Write 700 words on an explanatory or normative claim and a serious objection. Separate what the evidence establishes from what remains a philosophical inference.

records.title: Comparative-method workshop
records.source_text: Return to Wiredu. Audit one of your earlier comparisons for conceptual translation, selective evidence, and overgeneralization. Revise the argument rather than just adding a disclaimer.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words on the Menkiti–Gyekye debate, Du Bois and Fanon on a specified problem, or a precise Mills argument. Include a checked specialist source and a method note explaining the limits of your scope.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Interpret an unseen assigned passage and answer a new objection. Readiness requires contextual accuracy and a genuine argument, not recognition of author names. Remedy unsupported generalizations by narrowing the claim and locating direct evidence.

records.title: Meaning and reference
records.source_text: Frege and Russell. Analyze an informative identity and a definite description. Produce a formalization with a prose account of what it clarifies and what it leaves unresolved.

records.title: Names and necessity
records.source_text: Kripke Lecture I. Distinguish rigid designation, epistemic certainty, and necessity. Write 700 words on one argument against a descriptive account; do not assess Lecture III claims that have not been assigned.

records.title: Mind and explanation
records.source_text: Ryle I and Putnam. Compare category-error and functionalist strategies. Construct an original multiple-realization example and explain why it matters.

records.title: Intelligence and understanding
records.source_text: Turing and Searle. Separate an operational test from a theory of consciousness. Reconstruct the Chinese Room and the systems reply as presented in the article. Write a 700-word objection and response.

records.title: Experience and physicalism
records.source_text: Nagel and Jackson. Identify the epistemic and metaphysical premises separately. Compare an ability/knowledge reply from a checked scholarly overview; do not present that overview as an assigned primary Lewis paper.

records.title: Integrative workshop
records.source_text: Select one connection between language, understanding, and consciousness. Produce a 1,000-word debate map with two rival views and one unresolved question. This is preparation for the essay, not an additional final paper.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words evaluating a single argument from the course. Keep interpretive fidelity separate from your proposed improvement. Use one verified secondary source and a new case.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Interpret a new passage, solve a new reference/description problem, and defend the paper against a changed case. If formalism obscures meaning, translate every symbol back into English before retesting.

records.title: Art, imitation, and evidence
records.source_text: Republic X 595a–608b. Analyze the argument against imitation and its target; choose two works for later comparison and record reliable metadata.

records.title: Hume on taste
records.source_text: Whole essay. Reconstruct the standard and the qualified judge. Write 600 words on whether the account is circular or culturally narrow.

records.title: Kant on beauty
records.source_text: §§1–22. Explain the four moments with distinct examples, then test one claim about disinterest or universality. Avoid equating “disinterested” with uninterested.

records.title: Defining art
records.source_text: Weitz and Danto. Compare open-concept and artworld strategies. PC activity: classify a difficult example under both and explain what evidence is needed.

records.title: Categories and perception
records.source_text: Walton. Reinterpret one work under two categories, distinguishing what actually changes in experience from what the theory predicts.

records.title: Case essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words defending a theory-guided judgment or classification of a specified work, addressing a serious rival reading. Include provenance and reproduction limitations.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Analyze an unfamiliar work with sufficient contextual information, reconstruct one course argument, and respond to a new objection. Revise if a verdict depends on missing facts. Readiness concerns justified interpretation, not sharing the tutor’s taste.

records.title: Pragmatist method
records.source_text: James II and VI. Apply the pragmatic maxim to a carefully bounded dispute, then test a common caricature. Write 700 words on what James’s truth claim does and does not assert.

records.title: Organism and environment
records.source_text: Dewey’s article. Map the critique of a stimulus–response sequence and explain its philosophical significance without treating the article as contemporary neuroscience.

records.title: Phenomenological reduction
records.source_text: Husserl I–II. Write a 600-word explanation of the methodological move and a separate question about its justification. Keep description and argument visibly distinct.

records.title: Embodied experience
records.source_text: Merleau-Ponty Preface. Perform a short, safe description of ordinary perception, then distinguish your observation from claims attributed to the text. No simulation establishes a universal psychological law.

records.title: Freedom and ambiguity
records.source_text: Sartre’s lecture and Beauvoir Part I. Compare a precise claim about freedom, situation, or responsibility, with textual evidence and an objection.

records.title: Faith and the ethical
records.source_text: Kierkegaard Problema I and its editorial context. Explain the pseudonymous presentation and teleological suspension claim. Distinguish understanding the argument from endorsing its conclusion.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words on one methodological dispute or a bounded comparison between two assigned texts. Use genre-appropriate criteria: faithful description, interpretive evidence, and the inferential work done by the example.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Interpret a new passage and explain what would count as a successful objection within that method. Remedy caricatures by reconstructing the author’s question before comparing conclusions.

records.title: Family and the scope of justice
records.source_text: Okin 1 and 8. Identify the argument about the family and background assumptions of a theory of justice. Write a 700-word analysis of one claim.

records.title: Feminist method and difference
records.source_text: hooks 1–2. Reconstruct the critique of the movement and its audience; explain what follows for political method. Avoid treating any one author as all feminist philosophy.

records.title: Structural injustice
records.source_text: Young chapter 2. Apply two distinct forms of oppression to a documented case and explain the limits of the evidence. A fictional teaching case is acceptable if clearly labelled.

records.title: Equality and relationships
records.source_text: Anderson’s article. Map the objection to luck egalitarianism and the alternative. Write 800 words defending or challenging one inference with an original case.

records.title: Beyond human institutions
records.source_text: Singer’s chapter 1 and Leopold’s essay. Compare the unit of moral concern, the role of consequences, and conflicts within each approach. Do not make the approaches agree by removing their controversial commitments.

records.title: Method and idealization
records.source_text: Mills’s article. Audit an earlier case analysis for assumptions that conceal exclusion or historical conditions.

records.title: Essay and revision
records.source_text: Write 2,000–2,400 words on a single course dispute, including a documented or explicitly hypothetical case and the strongest objection. Separate empirical uncertainty from normative disagreement.

records.title: Assessment and delayed check
records.source_text: Analyze a changed case and interpret an unseen assigned passage. Readiness requires a defensible argument and careful scope, not adopting a prescribed political position.

records.title: Default and alternative paper prompts
records.source_text: Default paper prompt: “Does the argument I select establish a necessary condition for consciousness, or only a reason for uncertainty?” Alternative: “What would count as evidence against the systems reply in a specified model of understanding?” A tool’s fluent answer is an object of analysis, not empirical proof of its internal state. Any informal demonstration must be labelled illustrative, with no claim that a few prompts constitute a scientific experiment.

records.title: Default and alternative paper prompts
records.source_text: Default paper prompt: “Does my proposed interpretation make the Mengzi–Xunzi disagreement substantive rather than merely verbal?” Alternative: “Can Aristotle’s account clarify one feature of cultivation without distorting the Chinese text?” Include a short translation note and one counterexample that tests your actual conclusion.

records.title: Default and alternative paper prompts
records.source_text: Default paper prompt: “Does one specified framework explain an exclusion case that another misses, and why?” Alternative: “Does a proposed remedy answer the identified epistemic wrong without creating a different injustice?” Use a documented case with restrained factual claims or a clearly hypothetical case. Do not make allegations about identifiable people as an exercise.

records.title: Proposal and feasibility
records.source_text: Write 800–1,000 words containing the question, significance, provisional claim, method, strongest anticipated objection, source needs, and exclusions. State why the question can be answered within the paper. The proposal is ready only when essential sources can actually be read.

records.title: Literature and source dossier
records.source_text: Build an annotated bibliography of the sources that genuinely bear on the question. A likely working set is eight to twelve relevant items, including sources already studied in the advanced seminar; relevance governs the count. Read the portions that bear on the question, not automatically eight to twelve whole books. Plan roughly forty to seventy pages of additional close reading in this phase, plus rechecking earlier notes and writing annotations. If the argument requires more new reading, enlarge the logged budget or narrow the question rather than pretend that a whole source has been read. For each, record a complete citation, legal access route, exact relevant pages/sections, the claim used, and whether you read the whole item or only a defined portion. Include foundational arguments, a serious competing view, and current scholarship where relevant. Verify every quotation.

records.title: Argument plan and trial section
records.source_text: Make a detailed outline and write a 1,000-word central section. Test the main inference before writing the entire paper. If it fails, revise the question rather than hide the failure in background exposition.

records.title: Full first draft
records.source_text: Write the complete paper in your own words. Separate exposition from defense, and make the contribution visible. Include citations and a provisional bibliography; do not postpone all sourcing to the end.

records.title: Critical review
records.source_text: Request a focused human review if available and chosen; otherwise arrange a skeptical source-bound review and label it provisional. Ask about the most serious interpretive error, the weakest inference, and the strongest objection. Write a response plan explaining which suggestions you will accept and why.

records.title: Substantive revision
records.source_text: Reorganize and rewrite where needed. Resolve citation issues, check every significant attribution, and remove claims beyond the evidence. Keep an explicit limitations section where appropriate. A revision memo explains the three most important changes.

records.title: Presentation and defense
records.source_text: Prepare a ten-to-fifteen-minute explanation and answer twenty-to-thirty minutes of unscripted questions or an equivalent accessible format. Include a challenge not rehearsed during drafting and an explanation of what would change your conclusion. Revise again if the defense exposes a substantive error.

records.title: Final portfolio and delayed synthesis
records.source_text: Submit the revised paper, bibliography, assistance declaration, revision memo, and selected earlier artifacts. Write a 1,000-word reflection comparing an early and late argument, identifying actual development and remaining gaps. After a pause, explain the project and apply its central distinction to a fresh case. These activities, including the final source audit, are within the 180-hour estimate.
